title: Protein Can Help Build and Preserve Muscle, But Eating More Has Its Limits - Nautilus
gist: High protein has become a marketing selling point from cereals to yoghurts, but the piece argues extra protein's benefit depends on baseline intake and muscle use: weightlifters and low-appetite older adults may benefit, while those already eating enough gain little.

insights.claim: High protein content has become a marketing selling point across food categories ranging from breakfast cereals to yoghurts.
insights.speaker: Dominic Farsi
insights.so_what: The high-protein labeling trend is a packaged-food growth lever; watch for consumer skepticism eroding its premium.
insights.quote: High protein content has become a selling point on foods ranging from breakfast cereals to yoghurts.

insights.claim: People who already eat enough protein may gain little from adding more, so choosing the highest-protein product is not automatically beneficial.
insights.speaker: Dominic Farsi
insights.so_what: Diminishing returns could cap demand for protein-fortified products among already-adequate consumers.
insights.quote: Someone already eating enough protein may gain little from adding more.

insights.claim: People who regularly lift weights may benefit from additional protein to support muscle growth.
insights.speaker: Dominic Farsi
insights.so_what: Strength-training consumers remain the core addressable market for protein supplements.

insights.claim: Older people with small appetites may need help getting enough protein to maintain strength, making them a distinct need-based segment.
insights.speaker: Dominic Farsi
insights.so_what: Aging populations represent a needs-driven market for protein supplementation and fortified foods.
insights.quote: An older person with a small appetite may need help getting enough to maintain strength.

insights.claim: The value of extra protein is framed as personal, depending on existing diet and how muscles are used, which informs choices between diet changes, supplements, or focusing on exercise.
insights.speaker: Dominic Farsi
insights.so_what: Personalized nutrition positioning may outcompete blanket high-protein claims.
